title: When the Monsoons Changed
subtitle: Monsoon Shadows over a Fading Bronze Age
era: Harappan decline and genetic evidence, c. 2200-1300 BCE
region: Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Dholavira, Rakhigarhi and the Ghaggar-Hakra region
moral: Endings are rarely single events, and survival can change form.

sources.citation: Y. Dixit, D.A. Hodell and C.A. Petrie, 'Abrupt weakening of the summer monsoon in northwest India ~4100 yr ago,' Geology 42 (2014)
L. Giosan et al., 'Fluvial landscapes of the Harappan civilization,' PNAS 109 (2012)
sources.note: River and monsoon landscape study of Harappan settlement.

sources.citation: V. Shinde et al., 'An Ancient Harappan Genome Lacks Ancestry from Steppe Pastoralists or Iranian Farmers,' Cell 179 (2019)
sources.note: First published ancient DNA from a Harappan burial at Rakhigarhi.

dialogue.text: When the monsoons changed, the great cities of the Indus did not fall in one night; they slowly loosened their grip on the earth, leaving memory in bricks, riverbeds, and bones.
For centuries before 2000 BCE, from Mohenjo-daro to Dholavira, a web of brick cities hummed with trade, craft, and order, nourished by monsoon rivers that rose and fell with the seasons.
But around the middle of the third millennium BCE, the sky itself began to change. Palaeoclimate records tell us the summer monsoon weakened in northwest India, altering rain and river alike.
In distant Kotla Dahar, a quiet lake kept the record: lighter shells, changing sediments. From these traces, modern scholars read a story of less rain, shorter floods, and stressed landscapes.
Along the Ghaggar-Hakra plains, broad channels shifted and thinned. Not in a single disaster, but over generations, the water that had drawn settlements now demanded they learn to bend or move.

The decline from about 2000 to 1700 BCE was no sudden fall. Neighbourhoods emptied, workshops shifted, new pottery styles appeared. Urban life loosened into smaller towns and villages that endured for centuries more.
Rakhigarhi, once a proud urban centre, changed with the age. By the Late Harappan phase, our Rakhigarhi Woman lived among humbler houses built around the bones of older, grander streets.
She could touch the past in every brick. Standardized baked blocks from an age of distant trade, and newer, rough mud-bricks born of thrift and adaptation to a different rhythm of water and work.

Around her, farmers hedged their bets. Wells went deeper, fields hugged surviving channels, and people diversified crops and crafts. Climate strained them, but climate alone did not dictate their fate.

Faraway trade routes faltered as rivers changed and partners in Mesopotamia faced their own troubles. Harappan merchants adjusted, scaled down, turned inward. The world tightened, but did not break overnight.

panels.shot: somber wide shot at burial ground

dialogue.text: When her time came, they buried her with care, as their forebears had done. No sign of massacre, no city in flames—only a community carrying its customs into a changing age.
Centuries later, Late Harappan villages also thinned. By around 1300 BCE, the last echoes of that urban tradition had scattered into new regional cultures across the subcontinent.
Then, in our own age, seekers of the past opened the earth at Rakhigarhi. From one grave, they lifted the fragile remains of the woman whose life had quietly bridged a fading world.
From her tooth, in a controlled clean room, scientists coaxed ancient DNA. A rare survival in India’s hot climate, it offered a direct glimpse into one Harappan life from four thousand years ago.

Her genome, published in 2019, showed ancestry tied to ancient Iran-related farmers and South Asian hunter-gatherers, but none from later Steppe pastoralist groups that would reach the subcontinent after her time.
This single genome cannot speak for a whole civilisation, nor can it fix every debate. Yet it quietly challenges simple tales of an invading horde sweeping away an older people in sudden violence.
Her bones and genes tell us of continuity and change, of local roots and wider links. They show that the end of the Indus cities was woven from climate, trade, politics, and human choices together.

Endings in history are rarely a single blow. In the Late Harappan world, survival changed its form: cities relaxed into villages, traditions bent and blended, and the story of India flowed on in new channels.
